title: Copyright-Registration Autopilot for AI Settlements
one_liner: Monthly bulk US copyright registration and an evidence vault for creators, so they are eligible when AI settlements and claims open.
customer: Newsletter writers, podcasters, photographers, illustrators and indie musicians, plus small publishers and labels, most of whom have never registered a work.
problem: In the Anthropic authors settlement (Sep 2025), only works with timely US registrations qualified, and new music and news suits (for example UMG and Sony against Suno, per the brief) follow the same logic. Registration also gates suing at all and statutory damages. Most independent creators skip it because of fees and friction, which puts them at the back of every claims line.
solution: OAuth into Substack, Beehiiv, Ghost, Bandcamp and portfolio storage. The service assembles the right group registrations (short online literary works, photographs, unpublished works, albums), files them with the Copyright Office, tracks registration numbers and deposit copies, and keeps a tamper-evident vault of first-publication evidence. A claims desk alerts users when a settlement or class definition matches their registered works. Has an attorney review the workflow.
why_now: The 2025-2026 AI settlements and suits made registration status the gating asset. Creator demand for anything that pays them from AI is high, and the Suno-Warner settlement shows deals are landing.
revenue_model: $19-39/month plus pass-through Copyright Office fees, a $99 first-year catch-up batch, and an optional 10% of recovered settlement payouts through the claims desk.
non_obvious_insight: Class-action money goes to the paperwork-ready. For an AI-era creator, registration status may be the most valuable and most neglected asset, and the boring gate is where a subscription business sits.
first_30_days: Partner with a copyright attorney to design the workflow. Pilot with 50 newsletter writers and 20 illustrators from creator communities, using a free 'AI-claims readiness audit' as the lead magnet.

title: Live Read-Aloud Rooms Staffed by Displaced Narrators
one_liner: Landline-friendly live group reading sessions led by professional audiobook narrators for isolated and low-vision elders, sold to agencies as a human alternative to free AI companion robots, with an attested 'human minutes' ledger.
customer: Area Agencies on Aging and state aging offices, senior-living operators, and Medicare Advantage or Medicaid plans buying social-isolation supplemental benefits. Families and libraries for the blind are a secondary channel.
problem: NY, FL and NJ now hand out ElliQ AI companions free, and 'loneliness reduction' is a funded policy goal, yet the buyer is buying synthetic contact. Meanwhile professional audiobook narrators are being squeezed by AI narration programs. Many isolated elders are on landlines, have low vision or fading attention, and cannot use apps or long-form video.
solution: Dial-in or smart-speaker reading rooms, 45 minutes each, 25-40 elders per room, with rooms by taste (mysteries, poetry, serialized novels, local history, faith). The narrator addresses listeners by name and takes requests. The platform logs attendance and issues a funder-facing 'verified live human minutes' report, which is the metric that a loneliness grant or plan benefit actually needs. Shared reading has a track record in dementia settings, so a memory-care track is included.
why_now: Governments are already in the market for loneliness tech and have discretionary budgets. AI narration has pushed skilled, warm voices into part-time work exactly as human-made is turning into a priced attribute. Older adults are adopting AI fast (23% of 65+ use ChatGPT), and a visible human alternative is a differentiator for buyers under pressure not to replace people with robots.
revenue_model: $35-45 per active elder per month, priced against ElliQ's $40 a month plus $250 upfront. Narrators earn about $45 per session, and a 30-person room yields roughly 40% gross margin. Contracts come from AAA and plan budgets on annual terms.
non_obvious_insight: The funder's real KPI is human contact minutes, not content. AI companions cannot honestly claim that ledger, but a narrator-led room can prove it. The scarce input is warm, trained voices, and AI has just made a pool of them cheap and underemployed.
first_30_days: Recruit 8 narrators from audiobook narrator communities and voice-actor unions. Run 3 free public rooms via a conference bridge and recruit elders through two county AAAs and a senior center. Collect attendance and self-reported loneliness scores and pitch the county AAA a $6-10k, three-month paid pilot.

title: Cross-Border Clearinghouse for VTuber Merch
one_liner: A duty-paid storefront and fulfillment rail for VTuber agencies that pre-sells to overseas fans and clears unsold Japanese inventory to them.
customer: Mid-size and independent VTuber and idol agencies (not Cover or Anycolor initially), plus overseas fans buying from a duty-paid storefront.
problem: Cover Corp's FY3/2026 revenue rose 13.7% but net profit fell 45.7%, hit by 1.8B yen of unsold merch and a 3.3B yen metaverse write-off. Overseas viewers are about 30% of viewership and roughly 10B yen of revenue, yet those fans face customs surprises, region-locked stores and 30-100% proxy markups.
solution: A global storefront and fulfillment layer with duty-paid shipping, pre-order demand aggregation, and Japanese warehouse partners. Overseas pre-order counts feed manufacturing quantities to reduce overproduction. Overstock is bought or consigned and resold to overseas fans with authenticity guarantees.
why_now: The US ended its $800 de minimis exemption in Aug 2025 and the EU is moving the same way, which breaks the old cheap-parcel proxy model. Hololive's profit drop is a public case study in overproduction.
revenue_model: 15-25% commission on gross merchandise value plus fulfillment fees, and 25-40% of wholesale margin on bought overstock.
non_obvious_insight: Overproduction in Japan and unmet demand overseas are two sides of one imbalance. Forecasts miss overseas demand because logistics hide it, so a clearinghouse converts waste into revenue and generates a better forecast from pre-orders.
first_30_days: Contact 10 small VTuber agencies and 3 Japanese merch producers. Launch a 50-SKU duty-paid shop for one agency. Line up a Japan-based fulfillment partner and pre-sell to an overseas fan community.

title: Proof-of-Review Receipts for AI-Using Professionals
one_liner: A tamper-evident record that a named, licensed human actually reviewed AI output, backed by planted-error vigilance tests, sold to firms and their malpractice carriers.
customer: Mid-size law firms, accounting firms and physician groups using AI drafting or scribes, and the malpractice and E&O carriers, MGAs and brokers underwriting AI use.
problem: Courts worldwide have issued about 1,490 decisions on AI-hallucinated filings (1,000+ in the US by May 2026), with sanctions up to $110k and the first suspensions. More than 60% of carriers now ask about AI use in underwriting, and some add AI endorsements or exclusions. Firms cannot prove that attorney review happened beyond a policy memo.
solution: A review layer (Word and Outlook add-in, EHR plug-in, browser extension) that logs what the AI produced, what the human changed, dwell time, automated cite-check results and sign-off. It also seeds a random slice of reviews with canary errors (a fake citation, a wrong dose in a test document) to measure whether reviewers really catch them. A signed monthly review-integrity report goes to the carrier for premium credit or endorsement eligibility.
why_now: AI-hallucination sanctions are growing by about eight cases a day. The EPIC 2026 claims survey shows carriers seeing more AI-related claims, and carriers are rewriting applications and endorsements now.
revenue_model: $30-80 per professional per month, carrier and broker partnerships (revenue share on premium credits), and a cite-check add-on.
non_obvious_insight: The weak link is automation complacency, not just model hallucination. You can measure complacency the way airports measure screener vigilance, by planting known-bad items. Insurers will pay for measured human vigilance because it is a rating factor.
first_30_days: Partner with one legal-malpractice MGA or broker and 10 small firms (5-50 lawyers) through state-bar CLE channels. Ship a Word add-in that logs review and checks citations. Pilot canary errors with written consent.

title: AI-Guided Feline Heart Screening by Technicians
one_liner: Handheld ultrasound with AI probe guidance lets technicians capture heart clips on cats, with remote cardiologist over-read making HCM screening a routine add-on instead of a referral.
customer: General-practice clinics (senior and pre-anesthetic cats), breeders of at-risk breeds, and shelters; later insurers.
problem: Feline hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is common and often silent until clot or heart failure. Screening needs a cardiologist's echo, which is scarce and costs a few hundred dollars, so most cats are never screened. Cat households are growing (53M) and the vet workforce is not.
solution: Existing vet-priced handheld probes, a guidance app that prompts standard views and rejects poor clips (trained on cardiologist-labeled data), and a board-certified over-read within 24 hours with next-step recommendations. Sold as a 'senior cat heart check' and a breeder program.
why_now: AI acquisition guidance for novices has been proven in human echo, handheld ultrasound is cheap, vision models are strong, and remote reading is a way to stretch scarce cardiologists while techs take on more scope.
revenue_model: $60-90 per over-read, probe leasing at about $199 per month, and breeder program fees.
non_obvious_insight: The product is not AI diagnosis; it is AI acquisition guidance so a technician can collect usable images. The scarce resource is the cardiologist's time, so pooling over-reads creates the leverage, and the resulting longitudinal dataset improves guidance and screening protocols.
first_30_days: Sign 1-2 board-certified cardiologists on a per-read basis. Equip 5 clinics with handheld probes and run 100 screening scans. Measure the share of diagnostic-quality clips, then sell a $99 senior cat heart check.

title: Warranty Clock Recovery Audits for Idle Halls
one_liner: A contingency-fee service that finds and files the warranty claims on energized-but-empty data halls before OEM warranty clocks silently expire.
customer: Colocation developers, powered-shell landlords, neocloud operators and enterprise owners with phased or delayed-tenant builds, especially those with halls commissioned 6-14 months ago and not yet loaded. The owner pays a percentage of recovered value, plus an optional per-asset tracking subscription.
problem: Warranty clocks on generators, UPS systems, chillers, CRAH/CDUs, switchgear, and batteries usually start at shipment or startup, not when a tenant loads the hall. With delayed leases and mid-build AI redesigns, halls sit energized and idle for months. Many defects only show under real load (UPS capacitors, chiller compressors, wet-stacking gensets, breaker trip curves, coolant chemistry). By the time the tenant ramps, the warranty has expired. The turnover package is 50,000+ pages of PDFs that ops never reads, the punch-list deferrals are lost, and OEM maintenance records required to keep coverage valid are often missing. Nobody owns the clock.
solution: Ingest POs, OEM warranty terms, startup sheets, Cx reports, shipping documents and maintenance logs with an LLM pipeline to build a serial-number-level warranty ledger with real expiry dates and voiding conditions. Flag anything expiring within 120 days. Run a targeted load-dependent-defect inspection before expiry (thermography, oil and coolant samples, capacitor and battery checks, breaker testing). File claims, negotiate warranty start-date deferrals or extensions with the OEM while leverage still exists, and fix missing maintenance-record gaps. For new builds, sell a PO-stage clause pack that defers warranty start to beneficial occupancy.
why_now: There is a glut of speculative shells and delayed tenant handoffs. Reporting in 2026 shows close to half of planned US builds slipping, with only about a third of 2026 target capacity under active construction. That means many halls are powered, commissioned and idle. Equipment was bought at peak prices with tariffs on steel, aluminum and copper, so each lapsed warranty is worth more. LLMs can now read messy closeout binders cheaply, which was the labor bottleneck for audits like this.
revenue_model: 25-30% of recovered value or avoided cost on claims and negotiated extensions, no fee if nothing is recovered. Optional $150-400 per asset per year tracking subscription. $15K-40K fixed-fee closeout audits for owners who want certainty. PO-stage clause-pack consulting for developers.
non_obvious_insight: The warranty is the only major asset on a data center balance sheet that expires silently. OEMs will defer warranty start dates at PO time, but almost no one negotiates it because the project team is fighting for delivery slots, not paperwork. After the fact, the owner's ops team inherits the docs with no idea when the clocks started. The money is in the punch-list items that were 'to be fixed later' and the load-dependent defects that only appear after the hall is finally used.
first_30_days: Find 3 owner-operators through PM and Cx network contacts with halls energized 8-11 months ago and not fully loaded. Offer a free 10-day scan of their closeout binders in exchange for a contingency agreement on any claims. Build the extraction pipeline on real binders (gensets, UPS, chillers first). Deliver a 'expiring within 90 days' hit list and file the first claims before the first invoice.

title: Ruling-Backed Tariff Engineering for Product Brands
one_liner: A productized design-and-ruling service that helps mid-market brands legitimately re-spec products across tariff-line boundaries and locks the result in with a CBP binding ruling.
customer: Mid-market consumer and industrial product brands with $10-100M in revenue and at least $1-2M in annual duty spend: footwear, bags, apparel accessories, home goods, hardware, e-bike and powersports parts, and other products with metal components.
problem: Adjacent tariff lines can differ by tens of percentage points, and the 2025-26 regime made the gaps bigger. Section 232 metals lists keep expanding and being recalibrated, and copper smelt-and-cast reporting started July 30, 2026. Yet brokers are asked for a classification only after the tooling is cut and the design is frozen. Product teams never learn that a small change in materials, construction, packaging or set composition can legally change the line. Importers also avoid asking CBP for rulings, assuming it is slow or risky.
solution: Sell two steps. First, a fixed-fee HTS boundary audit: map the top SKUs to the classification tests, spec thresholds and comparable public CBP rulings that determine the line, and list the small design or packaging changes that would legitimately move each one. Second, an engineering sprint with the supplier that documents the changed product and files a CBP binding ruling request under 19 CFR Part 177. The deliverable is a ruling letter, which is a lasting shield for reasonable-care defense. Add a ruling-watch subscription that alerts brands when CBP issues a ruling on competitor or adjacent products.
why_now: The IEEPA reversal shifted the burden to product-specific tariffs (Section 232 and 301) where design details matter. The July 2026 copper reporting and the rewritten 232 valuation rules make product composition a compliance and cost variable. Brands are in a rare window when rate spreads are large enough that redesign pays for itself in one production run.
revenue_model: $4,500 boundary audit for five SKUs; $18-35k per engineering sprint including ruling preparation and filing; optional success fee of about 10% of first-year duty savings, capped. Ruling-watch subscription of $500-$2,000 a month.
non_obvious_insight: Classification turns on physical facts of the article as imported, and those facts are set by designers, not brokers. The most valuable document in a tariff war is a dull letter from CBP's ruling office, and requests cost nothing to file. Tariff engineering is legal when the product really changes, and it requires evidence, which is where a broker's habit of documenting everything matters. Trade lawyers do this ad hoc for large clients, but nobody packages it for mid-market brands at design stage.
first_30_days: Pick two verticals with high design freedom and large rate spreads. Use public CBP rulings to build a boundary map for a prospect's own top SKU as a free sample. Cold-email 40 product, sourcing and COO leads at $10-100M brands with their own sample map. Sell three $4,500 boundary audits and use them to select the first ruling filings. Sign a trade lawyer as reviewing counsel on the ruling requests.

title: Passive Wellness Alerts From Water Meter Patterns
one_liner: A subscription that texts an adult child, or their parent's home-care agency, when an older person living alone has no expected water activity: no wearable, no camera, just the meter that is already on the house.
customer: Adult children of seniors who live alone ($12-19 per month). Home-care agencies and Area Agencies on Aging, which pay about $15-25 per client per month for a passive check on clients between visits. Later, Medicare Advantage plans offering supplemental benefits, at a per-member-per-month rate. Utilities are the channel partner, not the main payer.
problem: Roughly a quarter or more of Americans aged 65 and older live alone. Existing safety products get abandoned: pendants are left on the nightstand, wearables aren't charged, and cameras feel like surveillance and get unplugged. Families end up making anxious phone calls. Meanwhile the utility already has hour-level (or finer) consumption data from its smart meter, used only for bill disputes and leak alerts. Nobody has to wear or charge a meter.
solution: Learn each household's rhythm from interval water data: first use in the morning, number of daily events, typical overnight quiet. Alert on: no water event by the person's usual time plus a buffer, unusually long or repeated overnight use (possible wandering or confusion), continuous flow (leak or overflow), and sudden spikes. Escalate by text to a family member, then to a designated neighbor or a non-emergency wellness-check partner. Two data paths. Path A is a $40-bill-of-materials clamp-on or pulse reader on the customer's own meter, installed in 15 minutes by a caregiver, which needs no utility integration. Path B is a customer-consented feed from the utility's smart-meter system, with no hardware and utility co-branding. Leak protection is a free bonus that sells the same product to the utility.
why_now: The oldest baby boomers are now in their 80s, and 'Peak 65' has meant around 4 million Americans turning 65 every year through 2027. Home-care labor is scarce, so agencies need passive tools that extend a caregiver's reach. Smart-meter adoption among mid-size and large water utilities is now high, and those utilities are looking for customer-engagement wins after the billing complaints that followed rollouts. Green Button-style customer-directed data sharing exists for electricity but is almost absent for water. LLMs can also explain a pattern change in plain language to worried families.
revenue_model: Family subscription of $12-19 per month, plus optional hardware at cost or $49. B2B2C contracts with home-care agencies at $15-25 per client per month. Revenue share or flat fees from utilities per opted-in household. Later, Medicare Advantage supplemental-benefit contracts.
non_obvious_insight: Water use is the most honest sign of life in a house. Nobody can skip flushing for 36 hours, and it can't be faked, forgotten or unplugged. Japan's Zojirushi 'mimamori' kettle proved families will pay for a signal from an ordinary appliance. A utility meter is the same idea at the level of the whole house, and utilities are sitting on the data with no product.
first_30_days: Partner with two or three local home-care agencies and an Area Agency on Aging. Recruit 30 consenting seniors or families through caregiver support groups and Facebook groups for adult children. Install pulse or clamp-on readers on meters that support them, and run a 30-day baseline. Alert families by text and measure false-alarm and helpfulness rates. In parallel, approach one mid-size smart-meter utility with an opt-in pilot: consented data sharing at no cost, with the utility's logo on the program. Charge families $15 per month from day 31.

title: Sold-Out-of-Trust Radar for Floorplan Lenders
one_liner: Catch dealers that sell floored cars and pocket the payoff by watching the one signal an F&I insider knows can't be hidden: the VIN disappears from public listings but the floorplan payoff never arrives.
customer: Floorplan lenders and their auditors: independent floorplan companies, captive finance arms, regional banks and credit unions with dealer lines, and warehouse lenders that fund subprime and buy-here-pay-here dealers. Pay $15 to $30 per monitored dealer per month plus enterprise data fees.
problem: A dealer sells out of trust when it sells a floored car and does not pay the lender's payoff on time. It is how small cash squeezes become fraud. Ford and Stellantis are in court against Sky Auto Mall over exactly this, and floorplan use is heavier with inventory at roughly 88 days' supply and rates at SOFR plus 200 to 400 bps. Lenders police it with periodic on-site audits (monthly, quarterly or random), so a dealer can sell for weeks before anyone looks. The dealer's own delay makes it worse, since contracts in transit stretch to a week or more before the lender funds, so honest and dishonest dealers look identical in the books.
solution: Daily VIN-level monitoring of each lender's floored inventory against public and licensed listing feeds from the dealer's site and the major marketplaces. When a floored VIN disappears from listings, the tool starts a clock. It cross-checks against lender-provided payoff events and, where available, title and registration transactions and electronic lien releases. If no payoff shows within the expected window (about 7 to 10 days for a clean deal, longer for slow lenders), it flags the dealer and VIN and ranks risk by dealer history and how many VINs are in the queue. Flags trigger a spot audit or a curtailment call. A dealer-facing version shows honest dealers exactly which VINs look 'unpaid' so they can fix processing before the lender calls, and it doubles as an early-warning feed for warehouse lenders.
why_now: Sept 2025's Tricolor and PrimaLend collapses put double-pledged collateral and verification failures in front of every subprime lender and their investors. In March 2026 Ford and Stellantis were still litigating floorplan fraud against Sky Auto Mall. Rising inventory and higher rates increase floorplan reliance. Public listing feeds and cheap LLM data extraction make VIN-level monitoring practical for a team of three.
revenue_model: Per-dealer monthly monitoring fee, a per-alert fee on confirmed cases, and enterprise data licensing to captives and ABS or warehouse investors. Upsell: a contracts-in-transit tracker that gives dealers a lender-verified funding timeline and later powers same-day advances against verified contracts.
non_obvious_insight: The only place SOT cannot hide is the retail listing. A dealer will lie about payoffs, backdate titles and pay one lender with another's money, but it still has to take a car off its website when it sells it, because customers and marketplaces punish stale listings. Auditors check what is on the lot; nobody checks what left the internet. An F&I person knows this from watching sold cars vanish from the site the same day the deal is signed, and from knowing how long a funded payoff should really take.
first_30_days: Build a scraper for a pilot set of 50 dealer inventory pages and a listing-history log. Backtest on cases visible in public court filings (the Sky Auto Mall filings and a handful of others) to show the signal would have fired weeks earlier. Approach three small independent floorplan lenders and two credit unions with dealer floorplan lines, offer a free 60-day pilot on their books, and charge $20 per dealer per month after proving at least one real catch.

title: One Guide, Twelve Languages: Live-Dubbed Tours
one_liner: The guide speaks once and each guest hears their own language in low-latency synthesised audio, so mixed-language groups share one guide and cities see fewer, fuller groups.
customer: Independent guides, small tour operators and shore-excursion companies in cities that cap groups (Venice, Rome, Florence, Amsterdam, Kyoto), plus guide associations and municipalities.
problem: Language-siloed tours multiply the number of groups on the same street, and group-size caps and guide quotas bind. Guides cannot fill rare-language tours, and whisper systems only amplify the guide's voice.
solution: Guide microphone to live speech translation to each guest's phone, joined by QR with no app install, with per-listener language choice, a glossary of place names, an offline fallback, headcount tools and translated questions back to the guide. Sell a clip mic and hub kit plus per-tour credits.
why_now: Real-time speech-to-speech translation became good enough in 2025 (consumer earbuds now offer live translation and APIs offer realtime speech), eSIM and 5G make connectivity easy, and cities are tightening group caps.
revenue_model: USD 39-99 per guide per month or USD 1-2 per guest, USD 150 kits and municipal licences.
non_obvious_insight: Language silos are a hidden multiplier of overtourism. Merging groups cuts the number of groups without cutting visitors, so guides earn more and cities become allies and customers.
first_30_days: Recruit 20 guides in Rome and Florence, pilot two-language tours then four, and measure latency and guest satisfaction. Approach the guide association with the pilot results.

title: Closed-School Science Labs Shipped to African Schools
one_liner: Take decommissioned lab benches, microscopes, fume hoods and Chromebooks from US schools being closed, refurbish them into container-sized lab packages with a practical-exam curriculum, and sell them to private secondary schools in East and West Africa.
customer: Buyers are private and faith-based secondary school networks in Kenya, Uganda, Nigeria and Ghana, paying $8-15k per lab package. Sellers are US districts, charters and private schools that are closing and want fast, lawful disposal at low cost.
problem: More than 1,000 US public schools closed in 2025-26. Chicago alone has 135k empty seats, and Portland, Minneapolis and Albuquerque are queued behind it. Districts dispose of equipment through slow public-surplus auctions that recover pennies. Meanwhile African private schools running on tiny per-student budgets cannot afford lab equipment, even though national practical exams and newer competency-based curricula require it. A new lab costs $30-50k and takes months to import.
solution: Inventory soon-to-close buildings and remove complete science rooms, robotics kits, libraries and tested Chromebooks (with NIST-grade data wipes and export of working goods only). Bundle them into a 40-foot container with local installation, a practical-exam curriculum (matched to Kenyan, Nigerian or Ghanaian exam boards), a one-day teacher orientation, and a small annual refill of consumables. The district gets a disposal certificate and a possible donation receipt.
why_now: Closures are at a four-year high, so supply is predictable and geographically concentrated. The AI memory crunch, with memory now 30-40% of a device's bill of materials, has raised new-device prices and made used Chromebooks valuable. Distributed solar and batteries mean African schools can now run lab equipment and computers. As I understand it, Kenya's first competency-based senior-school cohort (2026) requires STEM practicals many schools cannot deliver.
revenue_model: Lab packages sell at $9-14k against a landed cost of $5-6k. A curriculum and refill subscription adds $600 per school per year. Districts pay a $1-3k decommissioning fee per closure in place of an auction consignment fee, or grant surplus title for free.
non_obvious_insight: A closing school is a fully assembled, curriculum-matched capital asset that public procurement can only sell by the pound, while the same asset is the binding constraint on practical-exam pass rates in low-fee African schools. The margin is in the bundle of equipment, practical curriculum and teacher orientation, not in the equipment, and that bundle is exactly what charity donation programs do not offer.
first_30_days: Pick one district and walk three soon-to-close buildings. Offer free removal of the first 10 science rooms in exchange for title to the equipment. Get letters of intent and 30% deposits from two or three African private-school owners through diaspora, church or school-association networks. Ship one container of two labs plus 200 tested Chromebooks. Line up an export broker and a data-wipe vendor before touching anything.

title: Buy Oil-Heat Dealers, Sell Heat Pumps
one_liner: Acquire retiring Northeast heating-oil dealers for their loyal customers and boiler-failure moments, run the fuel business as a cash annuity, and convert customers to heat pumps.
customer: Northeast homeowners heating with oil (from about 19% of homes in New York to 59% in Maine), income-qualified households with state and utility rebates, and dealer owners who want a succession exit.
problem: Oil-only dealers face policy-driven volume decline and aging owners with no successors, yet each holds 1,000 to 5,000 loyal customers with known equipment ages. Heat pump installers pay high customer-acquisition costs and lack trust. The federal 25C credit ended for systems placed in service after 2025, so state programs and CAC decide winners.
solution: Acquire small dealers, keep the local brand, drivers and techs. AI ops: a propensity model using tank size, burner age, delivery volume and home age to time an offer when a boiler is about to fail, virtual site surveys and load calcs from photos, automated rebate and financing paperwork, retraining of drivers and technicians for heat pump service, and route optimization to protect fuel cash flow during the transition. Sell 'heat-as-a-service' subscriptions with dual-fuel backup.
why_now: Post-2025, incentives shifted to state and utility programs (Massachusetts, New York, Maine and others), and HEEHRA rebates of up to $8,000 for income-qualified households continue where states have launched. Heat pump technology is mature for cold climates. Dealer owners are aging, and the customer relationship is the hard-to-buy asset.
revenue_model: Fuel margin as the cash cow, service contracts, heat pump installs at roughly $15k to $25k per job, and financing spreads. Acquisition financed with seller notes and SBA 7(a).
non_obvious_insight: Electrification's scarce asset is trust plus the moment a boiler dies. Oil dealers already own both, and they are the only local business that knows each home's system age and gets the 2 a.m. January call. Buy the relationship and use the declining fuel business to fund the conversion.
first_30_days: List 50 independent dealers within a two-hour radius from state oilheat associations. Approach five owners over 60 with seller-financed offers. Before buying, start as a white-label heat pump conversion partner that rev-shares with dealers on their customers, which can produce first revenue in 60 to 90 days.

title: Fitness-Adjusted Longevity Reports for Retirement Advisors
one_liner: A report that turns a client's own wearable and clinic metrics (VO2max, resting heart rate, grip strength, gait speed, sleep) into a life-expectancy range for Social Security claiming, annuity timing and withdrawal-rate decisions, sold to fee-only advisors.
customer: Fee-only RIAs and retirement planners serving affluent pre-retirees aged 58-70, at $75-150 per client report or $300-600 a month per advisor. Later customers are planning-software vendors and annuity carriers.
problem: Social Security is the largest lifetime asset most households own. Claiming at 70 instead of 62 raises the monthly benefit by roughly three-quarters, and the break-even sits around 80-83. That decision hinges on life expectancy, but planners use population tables. Clients in the top fitness quintile can plausibly outlive the average by several years, and the sedentary can be the opposite. Early claiming reportedly jumped in 2025 amid trust-fund and SSA-staffing fears, so many people are choosing blind.
solution: Adjust standard actuarial tables using published hazard ratios for cardiorespiratory fitness, gait speed, grip strength and resting-heart-rate trends. Output a range, not a point estimate, showing break-even age versus the chance of reaching it. Data comes in by consented export from Apple Health, Garmin or Oura and is processed locally. The PDF carries methodology and disclaimers written for advisor compliance, and it is explicitly not medical advice or insurance underwriting.
why_now: Consumer wearables now deliver near-clinical metrics, including FDA-cleared hypertension notifications on Apple Watch in 2025 and VO2max estimates on most premium devices. Basic planning software is being commoditized by AI, so advisors need differentiated inputs. A wave of early Social Security claiming in 2025 shows clients are making irreversible choices under fear. Advisors have avoided health data because of privacy concerns, but client-owned wearable data solves the consent problem.
revenue_model: Per-report pricing of $75-150, advisor subscriptions of $300-600 a month, and later white-label integrations with planning tools. Annuity carriers may pay for qualified leads.
non_obvious_insight: Planners have been told for decades to plan for longevity risk while seeing only age and sex, and wearables have quietly built the best individual mortality signal outside a hospital. A plus or minus 4-year shift is enough to move the claiming break-even, so precision is not needed. The buyer is the advisor, who needs a fiduciary-safe way to bring health into the conversation.
first_30_days: Build the calculator from published cohort studies on fitness and gait speed and a standard actuarial table, and have a consulting actuary review it for $3-5k. Run 30 free reports for eight advisors in fitness-forward niches such as physician-focused planners and FIRE planners. Collect feedback and objections. Then charge $99 a report, with no health data stored on your servers.

title: Court-Ready Satellite Emission Evidence for Litigators
one_liner: Expert-witness-grade reports that use hourly geostationary pollution data to document emission events at large industrial sources.
customer: Environmental plaintiffs' firms, community groups with litigation funders, state attorney general offices, and insurers or investors assessing pollution liability.
problem: As federal enforcement priorities shifted in 2025-26 (prior knowledge), private litigation and state action fill the gap. Those actors need independent, admissible evidence, and most cannot interpret satellite data.
solution: Case-specific 'Emission Event Reports' for large point sources (power plants, refineries, LNG terminals, petrochemical complexes). They combine hourly NO2, SO2 and HCHO enhancements from geostationary sounders (NASA TEMPO in North America, Sentinel-4 in Europe), wind reanalysis and thermal flare data, with documented chain of custody and academic expert witnesses.
why_now: Hourly pollution monitoring from geostationary orbit is new: TEMPO has been operating since 2023-24 and Sentinel-4 launched in 2025. Regulatory retreat drives demand for private evidence.
revenue_model: $15-60k per case report. Retainer for firms with recurring dockets. Expert-testimony fees.
non_obvious_insight: Litigation budgets grow when regulation shrinks. A method that survives a Daubert challenge is a defensible moat, because courts reward the first tested method.
first_30_days: Partner with an atmospheric scientist willing to serve as expert. Build a report template on three well-known refinery or power-plant events. Present to five environmental plaintiffs' firms and one state AG office, and sign a first paid case.

title: Retired Operators as Fractional Rural Water Chiefs
one_liner: A cooperative of retired licensed water operators, each serving as the certified 'operator in responsible charge' for several tiny water systems remotely plus monthly visits, while converting their tacit knowledge into digital manuals.
customer: Small community water systems under about 3,300 people (councils, water districts, mobile-home park owners, county utilities). State rural water associations and engineering firms refer them. Each pays a $2.5-5k/month retainer.
problem: About a third of the water workforce is eligible to retire within a decade, and tiny systems cannot compete for certified operators. No software fixes 'nobody with a license answers the phone at 2 a.m.' PFAS initial monitoring is due in 2027, the lead action level tightens to 0.010 mg/L on Nov 1, 2027, and nitrate hits small farm-belt systems hardest. Meanwhile 60-72-year-old operators want part-time income, autonomy and purpose.
solution: Recruit retirees holding Grade 2-4 certifications. Each covers 3-5 systems using remote SCADA and camera access, a compliance calendar (sampling, PFAS monitoring, lead-inventory reporting, consumer confidence reports) and a shared on-call rotation inside the co-op. Every operator records an 'exit interview' that becomes site-specific SOPs (which valve sticks, which well drops in August). A young apprentice is attached to each cluster so succession is built in. The co-op keeps 25-30%.
why_now: 2027 PFAS and lead-rule deadlines are close, and $7.2B of FY2026 State Revolving Fund money flows to systems that must show capable operations. Boomer retirements are peaking. Federal technical capacity is shrinking (EPA's research office was eliminated in 2026), and small systems are left on their own.
revenue_model: $2.5-5k per system per month retainer, of which the co-op keeps 25-30% and the operator earns roughly $30-50k a year part-time. One-off compliance projects (PFAS sampling programs, lead service line inventories) add $5-20k each.
non_obvious_insight: Tiny systems do not need 'AI SCADA'. They need one accountable licensed human, and the only growing supply of licensed operators is retirees. Many states let one certified operator be in responsible charge of several small systems (rules vary by state and need checking). The retiree's tacit local knowledge is the real asset being lost.
first_30_days: Partner with the state Rural Water Association and get the drinking-water program's list of systems with operator-certification violations. Recruit 8 retired operators through the association newsletter and conference. Sign 3 systems on 90-day trial retainers.

title: Lifeboat for Students of Closing Colleges
one_liner: A transfer-rescue service that maps every credit of a closing college's students into a receiving school's degree requirements, paid flat-fee by institutions and states, free to students.
customer: Payers: closing or distressed private colleges (which must file teach-out plans), state higher-ed agencies and accreditors, and regional receiving colleges that want transfer enrollment. Users: students at the closing school, roughly 500 to 3,000 per small college.
problem: When a small college closes, teach-out deals are improvised. Nursing, education and arts credits often fail to map. Students face a murky choice, because entering a teach-out forfeits closed-school loan discharge. Transcripts become hard to get, and many students simply stop out. One tally counts nine college closures in 2026, and Philadelphia Fed modeling points to dozens more.
solution: Within a week of an announced closure, ingest the catalog, syllabi and transcripts into a credit-mapping engine and produce course-by-course equivalency offers from 3 to 5 receiving schools. Give each student a lifeboat file: credits accepted, remaining requirements, time to degree, net price, and the teach-out versus transfer versus loan-discharge tradeoff, in plain language. Add written articulation letters from receiving schools, warm handoffs to admissions, and transcript custody. Offer a paid advocacy tier for credit-denial appeals.
why_now: The US high-school graduating class peaked in 2025 (about 3.9M) and shrinks about 13% by 2041, so the tuition-dependent-college shakeout is just starting. LLMs can now match syllabi to course equivalencies in hours, work that used to take registrars weeks per student. Receiving schools are hungry for transfer enrollment and closing schools have no bandwidth.
revenue_model: Flat fees only: a closure-response engagement ($25k to $75k) paid by the closing school, its state agency or a consortium; an annual credit-mapping and closure-readiness subscription ($30k to $100k) from receiving colleges; and a $149 to $299 student advocacy add-on. Do not charge per enrolled student, because the Higher Education Act's incentive-compensation ban prohibits enrollment bounties at Title IV schools (confirm with counsel).
non_obvious_insight: Students at a closing college are the highest-intent, highest-credit leads in higher education, but the bounty model that would normally monetize them is illegal, so the business must be paid for labor and neutrality instead. The moat is a growing corpus of verified course equivalencies plus being the trusted neutral on day one of a closure. Accreditors and state agencies need a vendor for teach-out compliance and do not want to be seen picking winners among rival colleges.
first_30_days: Build a tracker of announced and at-risk closures from accreditor notices and news. Pick the two nearest announced closures and offer their registrars and the state higher-ed agency a free pilot for one program (nursing or education). Line up 3 nearby receiving colleges' transfer directors. Hand-run LLM-assisted credit mapping on 50 students with a contract registrar reviewing, and deliver personal lifeboat files. Close the first flat-fee pilot with a receiving college or state agency, and publish a 'What to do when your college closes' guide for inbound.

title: Deorphanization Factory for AI-Nominated Enzymes
one_liner: A pooled-substrate, NGS-readout assay line that assigns function to hundreds of AI-nominated unknown enzymes per week for hundreds of dollars each.
customer: Genome-editing and enzyme-discovery companies, frontier-lab and academic agent-discovery teams, and industrial enzyme groups.
problem: Agent swarms nominate candidates far faster than anyone can characterize them. Anthropic's run went from 200,000+ reverse transcriptases to 20 candidates in 21 hours, yet the function of the resulting array-associated reverse transcriptase (ART) system is still unknown, with human validation and biochemical characterization as the bottleneck.
solution: Cell-free expression of candidates in 384-well format. Universal substrate panels of pooled, barcoded DNA and RNA oligo libraries are incubated with each enzyme. NGS reads out cutting, copying, ligating and editing, producing an automated activity 'passport' (substrate preferences, cofactors, temperature). Start with nucleic-acid-acting enzymes (nucleases, RTs, recombinases, ligases) where pooled NGS readout works, and add mass-spec panels for small-molecule enzymes later.
why_now: Anthropic's Sept 2026 ART discovery came with an explicit invitation to partner with other scientists. DNA synthesis is cheap, cell-free expression is mature, and agent discovery volumes are exploding.
revenue_model: $300-1,000 per enzyme passport, $50-250k discovery-partnership programs, and shared upside on licensed hits.
non_obvious_insight: Compute is commoditizing discovery, so the scarce step is cheap, standardized characterization. Pooled assays turn function into a read instead of a project. A passport format could become the exchange currency between agent discoverers and enzyme users.
first_30_days: Build a v0 pooled-substrate library and assay for reverse transcriptases and nucleases. Characterize 50 public candidates and publish the results. Approach 5 editing-tool companies and 3 academic agent-discovery groups with a $10k 50-enzyme pilot.

title: Post-Montgomery Walk-Around Audits for Freight Brokers
one_liner: A gig network of working and retired truckers who physically inspect the carriers a broker hires and hand back a lawyer-ready diligence file.
customer: Mid-size freight brokers and 3PLs ($50M to $1B gross bookings, 10 to 200 staff). The budget owner is the VP of compliance/risk or general counsel. Secondary buyers are contingent-auto and broker E&O underwriters, and shippers that run in-house brokerage.
problem: On May 14, 2026 the Supreme Court unanimously held in Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II that negligent-selection suits against brokers are not preempted by federal law. Brokers now have to prove they exercised reasonable care picking a carrier. Their vetting is entirely digital: SAFER lookups, insurance certificates, ID checks. Nobody has ever looked at the yard. Chameleon carriers with clean paperwork, fake addresses and fictitious pickups sail through, and so do genuinely dangerous small fleets. Verisk CargoNet put Q2 2026 theft losses at $304.6M, more than double Q2 2025, even though incident counts fell.
solution: Book a 45-minute physical walk-around of a carrier's listed terminal, yard or the driver's truck for $175 to $350. The trucker follows a 40-point protocol and shoots geo-stamped photo and video: steer tire tread and sidewall damage, brake chamber stroke, lights, ELD present and working, trailer age and VIN against registration, whether the address has a shop, lot and signage, and a two-minute driver interview. The broker gets a scored, reproducible report filed against the carrier ID. Upsells are a quarterly re-walk for top-tier carriers on high-risk lanes, and 'eyes on pickup', where a local trucker sits at the shipper's dock and confirms the right driver and truck load the freight (aimed at high-value copper, electronics and pharma loads). Build the checklist with a trucking-defense attorney so it holds up as evidence.
why_now: The May 2026 Montgomery ruling created a brand-new legal duty and every broker general counsel is scrambling. Insurers are repricing broker liability. Fictitious-pickup and impersonation theft keeps growing (Verisk CargoNet counted 158 fictitious pickups in Q2 2026). Meanwhile English-proficiency out-of-service enforcement and the February 2026 non-domiciled CDL rule are churning the small-carrier population, so more unknown carriers are entering the market.
revenue_model: Per-audit fees of $175 to $350, with the trucker keeping about 45 to 55%. Annual diligence-program retainers of $25k to $100k for brokers that want a defined audit cadence. Insurer premium-credit revenue share. A recurring data subscription selling carrier physical-condition scores back to the wider broker market.
non_obvious_insight: Any 20-year driver can size up a carrier's yard in 90 seconds. Chameleon outfits have one shiny truck, no shop, mismatched trailers, cords showing on the steer tires, and drivers who can't name their dispatcher. Digital vetting checks paperwork; a jury after Montgomery will ask 'did anyone actually look?' The product isn't a tool, it's discoverable proof of reasonable care. Drivers are already within 30 miles of nearly any carrier and sit idle on 34-hour restarts and at detention, so the inspector supply is cheaper and more credible than any consultancy's.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 vetted current and retired drivers from CDL forums and trucker Facebook groups and pay them per audit. Pay a trucking-defense attorney $2k to $3k to co-design the checklist and co-brand a 'Montgomery diligence protocol'. Build the capture app as a PWA with forms, geotagged photos and an auto-generated PDF. Cold-email 40 mid-size broker GCs and compliance heads, offering 5 pilot audits at $99 on their riskiest tier-3 carriers. Target 3 paying brokers by day 30 and 100 audits by month 3.

title: Solar Monitoring Data as Appliance Stethoscope
one_liner: Use the consumption data already sitting in installers' monitoring portals to spot dying air conditioners, resistance heat, hidden EVs and always-on pool pumps, then sell verified leads to HVAC and electrical contractors with a share back to the installer.
customer: HVAC and heat-pump contractors, EV-charger electricians and pool contractors pay per verified lead ($100-300). Installers earn a 20-30% revenue share. A later payer could be home-warranty companies and insurers who want early-failure signals.
problem: Post-2025, residential solar installers are short of revenue and sit on 500-5,000 past customers with monitoring already attached. HVAC contractors pay $150-500 per lead and spend most of their marketing budget in peak summer emergencies. Nobody mines the consumption stream (Enphase, SolarEdge and Tesla gateways record it every 5-15 minutes), where a failing compressor, a home heated by resistance strips or a new EV shows up clearly.
solution: Install-side product called Home Energy Plus. The installer emails past customers an opt-in for a free annual system checkup, connecting to their monitoring account through the OEM's API. An anomaly model flags: an AC drawing 25%+ more than on comparable weather days, short cycling, high winter baseline (resistance heat), overnight EV signature, pool pump running 24 hours. The customer gets a plain-language report ('your AC is likely low on refrigerant; a $99 tune-up now avoids a July failure'). Contractors bid for the lead in their service area, and the installer is paid a share. Homeowners can opt out at any time.
why_now: Federal 25C and 25D credits ended Dec 31, 2025, so heat-pump and HVAC contractors need intent-rich leads. Installers need recurring revenue from existing customers as new-install volume falls in 2026. OEM monitoring APIs are open to owner-authorized apps, and anomaly-detection models are cheap. Spring and fall shoulder seasons are when contractors most want planned replacements.
revenue_model: $100-300 per lead depending on trade and job size, split 70/30 with the installer. Optional $5-10 a month homeowner subscription for continuing reports. Later, sell early-failure signals to home-warranty companies at a per-home annual fee.
non_obvious_insight: An installer's monitoring portal is a stethoscope for the whole house, but installers use it only to answer why production is low. The consumption side is unlabeled and unused. Also, homeowners already trust the installer, and consent to share data is easiest to get from that relationship. A planned replacement in shoulder season is worth more to an HVAC company than an emergency job in July, because it fills idle crews.
first_30_days: Sign 3 installers with 1,000+ customers on Enphase or SolarEdge. Send the opt-in as a free annual checkup. Analyze 300 homes' historical data by hand and code up the first two signatures (AC and resistance heat). Produce 30 personalized reports. Sell the first 10 leads to two HVAC contractors at $150 each and measure close rate. Draft the consent and data-use terms with a privacy lawyer.

title: Keep-the-Laptop Severance With Certified Data Wipe
one_liner: At layoff time, employers offer departing remote workers the option to keep their own laptop, remotely wiped and reimaged with a certificate of erasure. The service recovers, refurbishes and resells the devices people don't keep.
customer: People Ops, IT and Finance leaders at companies running frequent small layoffs of remote and hybrid staff (roughly 10-500 people per round). They buy per device, often through outplacement firms and layoff counsel. The laid-off worker is the beneficiary.
problem: The 2026 labor market is low-fire, low-hire, so layoffs are frequent and small, and AI is the most-cited reason in Challenger data for five straight months. ITAD firms want pallets, not 40 laptops scattered across 40 homes. Unreturned devices are write-offs and data-exposure risks. Laid-off workers lose their tools just as they must freelance or job-hunt. Candidates are also increasingly expected to own capable hardware and AI tooling.
solution: On notice day the employee picks Keep or Return. Keep: the device is remotely wiped through the employer's MDM, reimaged clean with an open-source starter kit and optional AI-tool credits, and transferred at appraised fair value, which the employer can subsidize to zero (tax treatment confirmed with counsel). Return: prepaid box, chain-of-custody, refurbish and resell. The employer gets an asset-disposal record, a certificate of data erasure, and a reuse and Scope 3 report. Device-offboarding logistics vendors exist, but they sell shipping. None sells a keep-it option priced as severance.
why_now: DRAM prices are up about 400% since 2024, so even 3-year-old laptops carry real resale value. Amazon's January 2026 cut of about 16,000 corporate roles and AI-attributed cuts are normalizing rolling layoffs. Breaches such as the Mercor contractor data leak make loose devices a board-level concern. Employers face growing pressure to show soft-landing and circular-IT practices.
revenue_model: $40-90 per device fee from the employer. Resale margin on returned devices. Upsell of refurbished, warrantied laptop leases to laid-off freelancers. Referral fees from outplacement partners.
non_obvious_insight: The laptop is the one severance item worth much more to the employee than it costs the employer. It also removes the employer's biggest post-layoff liability, the unreturned device. Small, frequent AI-era layoffs create a long tail of single devices that the pallet-based ITAD industry ignores.
first_30_days: Pitch five HR and IT leaders through outplacement firms and employment-law contacts. Build the flow on existing MDM scripts (Jamf, Intune, Kandji) with a partner ITAD firm issuing certificates. Run a free pilot on one 50-person layoff, then charge about $60 per device. Publish the pilot's unreturned-device rate and cost per device as the case study.

title: Independent Safety Registry for Pet Medicines
one_liner: A neutral post-market surveillance system for veterinary drugs and biologics, built on pet-insurance claims plus owner-reported outcomes.
customer: Animal-health drugmakers and biologics developers (safety and medical-affairs teams) pay subscriptions. Pet insurers and MGAs pay for cost-effectiveness analytics. Vet groups and foundations use the public lookup.
problem: Vet adverse-event reporting is voluntary and underreported, and after the 2025 controversy over reported adverse events with anti-NGF antibody injections for canine osteoarthritis, owners and vets have no independent way to weigh safety signals. Pharma-run surveillance is not trusted. Insurers hold the only longitudinal cross-clinic data, yet are pushing 19.7% premium increases on 9% more animals without knowing which treatments reduce downstream claims. New modalities (mAbs, CGMs, long-acting insulins, oral oncology, and possibly a canine longevity drug) are arriving with no owner for outcomes data.
solution: A data trust that ingests de-identified claims from partner insurers and MGAs, optional practice-management extracts, and owner-reported outcomes gathered by a QR code at the clinic. It runs disproportionality signal detection in the style of FDA Sentinel. Outputs are (a) a safety dashboard for drug makers, (b) formulary and cost-effectiveness reports for insurers, and (c) a public 'what happened to dogs like mine' lookup for vets and owners.
why_now: Premiums rose 19.7% against 9% more animals, so insurers need loss-control insight. Big biologics and Loyal's longevity program (1,317 dogs in the STAY study, FDA acceptance of efficacy and safety sections) mean a wave of new launches. IDEXX buying CoVet shows workflow data is becoming a strategic asset, and independent players need a neutral alternative.
revenue_model: Pharma subscriptions of $60-250k per product family per year. Insurer analytics contracts of $50-150k per year. Custom post-marketing studies at $100-300k. A free public tier drives owner-reported data.
non_obvious_insight: Companion-animal medicine is the last big therapeutic area with no Sentinel-style system, and insurers are the only long-lived holders of cross-clinic data. After a public safety scare, drugmakers will pay for credibility that they cannot generate themselves, and insurers will pay for the same data to reduce claims.
first_30_days: Pitch small MGAs and startup insurers (hungry for analytics, less locked into data rules) on a free pilot in exchange for a data-sharing agreement. Build signal detection for the 10 most common drugs and biologics. Publish a public report on one hot topic, then sell two pharma safety leads a pilot subscription. Expect first revenue at month 4-6.

title: Real-Time Dental Benefits Texting Before December 31
one_liner: A dental-office tool that texts patients their actual remaining insurance dollars and a wallet card, filling the Q4 schedule that insurers' broken apps leave empty.
customer: Independent dental practices with 1-5 dentists, first those on Open Dental (open API) or Dentrix. The owner-dentist or office manager pays.
problem: Patients cannot find what benefit they have left. The insurers' own apps are among the worst-rated apps in the category. The Delta Dental Mobile App averages 1.49 stars over 1,809 ratings and United Concordia averages 2.48. Reviews describe 40+ login failures and complaints such as 'Doesn't let you see your EOB', 'Doesn't even show claims payments', 'App displays the wrong Member ID number' and 'Claims on app don't match claims on web'. Most benefit years reset on December 31, so treatment plans go unscheduled while the practice's front desk spends hours on the phone. Practice campaigns rely on benefit data stored in the practice software, which goes stale.
solution: Each night the tool runs real-time eligibility checks (X12 270/271 through an existing dental clearinghouse) for patients with accepted but unscheduled treatment. It calculates remaining annual maximum and deductible met. It then sends a personalized text with the patient's actual figure and a booking link, for example: 'You have $1,120 of your Delta Dental benefit left, and it expires Dec 31.' It also issues an Apple or Google Wallet pass with the insurance card and remaining balance. The front desk gets a ranked call list with expected production. There is no generative AI involved, and it works from live payer data, not from what the practice software last stored.
why_now: Today is Sept 28, 2026, so the Q4 use-it-or-lose-it window is open now and a pilot can run Oct 15 to Dec 20. Insurer apps still bounce users to a web browser to log in and show little data. Practice-software APIs and clearinghouse eligibility APIs are available to small vendors. A tool that ships in October can be measured in booked production before year end.
revenue_model: A free Q4 pilot with a 5% success fee on collected production from attributed appointments. After the pilot, $299/month flat per practice, or $199/month plus 3% of attributed production. Later add-ons: a January 'new benefits' campaign and a mid-year campaign for plans with fiscal-year resets.
non_obvious_insight: The insight is that the insurer's app is so bad that the dental office is the only interface patients trust, and the office has never been given real-time dollar figures in one place. The evidence is patient-side, not practice-side, so the practice-side demand (fuller Q4 schedules) still needs to be proven in the pilot. Evidence: Delta Dental Mobile App (1.49 stars, 1,809 ratings; 'Doesn't let you see your EOB'; login failures) at https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id1585628503 and its review feed at https://itunes.apple.com/us/rss/customerreviews/id=1585628503/sortby=mostrecent/xml. United Concordia Dental (2.48 stars; 'Doesn't recognize my member id'; EOB PDFs fail to load; no Apple Wallet ID) at https://itunes.apple.com/us/rss/customerreviews/id=522392221/sortby=mostrecent/xml. Practice-side friction: Dentrix reviewers cite 20+ hours on phone support during a forced migration at https://www.softwareadvice.com/dental/dentrix-profile/reviews/. The wedge sits beside the practice-management system, so the practice does not have to replace it.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: integrate the Open Dental API and one clearinghouse's eligibility API, and run the calculation on a test practice. Days 10-20: recruit 5 practices through Open Dental user forums and dentist Facebook groups, offering a free pilot with success-fee terms. Days 20-30: launch the first campaigns, tracking texts sent, appointments booked and production. Turn the results into a case study to sell more practices before mid-November and for next year's Q4.

title: Steeple Sites: Church Land for Satellite Ground Stations
one_liner: Master-lease deals with denominations to host satellite ground stations, gateways and RF sensors on steeples and surplus church land, sold to operators as a ready-made site portfolio.
customer: Ground-station-as-a-service networks, smallsat IoT and EO operators, and direct-to-cell or broadband constellation operators needing gateways. Congregations and dioceses are paid as hosts.
problem: Launch has flooded orbit (321 launches, 4,517 satellites deployed in 2025, about 10,400 Starlinks), and carrier partnerships are multiplying, so downlink capacity, gateways and RF-quiet sites are a constraint. Site acquisition is slow, one farm or roof at a time. Meanwhile congregations own tall, zoning-friendly structures and acreage, monthly attendance is stuck at about 33%, and many boards need rental income or surplus-property solutions.
solution: Negotiate master-lease templates with denominational property boards (diocesan or conference trustees). Pre-screen sites for line of sight, RF noise, power, fiber and zoning, and package them into portfolios by latitude and orbit. Partner integrators handle permitting and install, and congregations get a share.
why_now: The spectrum land-grab settled (EchoStar's $23B sale to AT&T closed in July 2026, and the $17B sale to SpaceX), MNO satellite deals are multiplying, and every country-level service needs terrestrial infrastructure. Congregation attendance has plateaued at a low level, so property decisions are live.
revenue_model: A $5-15k site-acquisition fee per signed site paid by the operator, 15-20% of lease revenue for the life of the lease, and install margin. Congregations target $6-24k per year (to be validated).
non_obvious_insight: The tower industry already proved steeples are leasable, tall, permitted and governed by a few trustees, but satellite site teams chase farmland. One denomination negotiation can unlock hundreds of sites, and a closing parish is a seller with time pressure.
first_30_days: Pick one diocese or conference with rural clusters and pitch a pro-bono pilot lease template. Screen 30 sites from imagery, and approach 3 ground-network or IoT operators with a shortlist for a country where they lack coverage. Charge a $2-5k site-survey fee for a 10-site report as the first revenue.

title: Certify Overseas Eldercare, Insure the Trip Home
one_liner: An independent audit standard, trial-stay program and medevac-backed membership for Americans moving parents into care in Mexico, the Philippines or Thailand.
customer: Adult children and spouses of middle-income seniors (assets $50-150k) who can't afford $6,300 a month in the US and can't get Medicaid. Elder-law and financial planners are the channel, and overseas operators buy audits.
problem: Assisted living and memory care abroad run $800-3,000 a month with 1:3 to 1:5 staffing claims, but there is no independent quality standard, Medicare doesn't work abroad, and families have no emergency evacuation or continuity-of-care plan. Trust, not price, blocks the market.
solution: US-run unannounced audits by bilingual RNs against a published rubric (staff ratios, medication safety, dementia protocols, fire, hospital proximity), with public scorecards. Add a 30-day trial-stay package, a membership bundling medevac and repatriation cover from a partner, US-physician telehealth oversight, and a family-visit travel budget.
why_now: The 2026 visa pause and TPS terminations closed the door on importing workers, and Wisconsin nursing homes wrote off apartments bought for overseas hires. Labor now moves the other way: patients go to the labor. Alongside the US costs ($114,975 a year for a nursing home, $74,400 for assisted living) and 90% occupancy, families are already exploring it.
revenue_model: Family-paid vetting and placement fee of $750-2,500 (families only, to avoid conflicts), $600-1,200 a year membership for evacuation cover and telehealth oversight, and separate operator-paid annual audit subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody thinks seniors will leave the US, but the buyer is a middle-income family choosing between $115k a year and a waitlist. The moat is a trusted third-party scorecard and a way home, the same trust layer that made medical tourism scalable.
first_30_days: Visit and score 10 facilities in one cluster (for example Lake Chapala/Guadalajara) with a nurse partner. Publish the rubric and first scorecards, pre-sell 30-day trial-stay packages to expat and retire-abroad groups, and sign a medevac partner.

title: Burn Boss: Prescribed Fire as a Service
one_liner: AI burn-window planning, permits, drone ignition crews and liability cover, so landowners can safely burn and insurers can pay for the risk reduction.
customer: Private landowners, ranchers, timber owners, prescribed burn associations, water districts and utilities in TX, OK, OR, CA and CO. Insurers and reinsurers later pay for outcomes.
problem: Prescribed fire is the most effective fuel-reduction tool and the least scaled. Barriers are burn-plan expertise, weather windows, permits and smoke filings, liability insurance and crew logistics, not the fire itself.
solution: Start with a burn-plan generator and weather-window alerts built on AI forecast ensembles, plus a permit and smoke-filing packet, sold to burn associations. Then add a drone-ignition operator network and a liability wrap through a partner MGA. Add verified before/after fuel maps that insurers can underwrite (check state burn-liability rules).
why_now: AI weather models became operational in 2025 (such as ECMWF's AIFS), drone aerial ignition has matured, and record reinsurance capital wants provable mitigation. Several states have been reforming burn liability law (verify).
revenue_model: $1-3K per burn plan, per-acre service fees, and later outcome payments from carriers or utilities.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is planning and liability, not fire. Insurers can pay because treated acreage lowers their probable maximum loss.
first_30_days: Join 3 burn associations, ship window alerts and the plan generator, and run 5 paid burns.
